topics.title: How many data types? Name them.
topics.html:
• Eight: seven primitives + one object type.
  • Primitives: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol.
  • Non-primitive: object (arrays, functions, dates, Map, Set — all objects).
typeof "hello"     // "string"
typeof 42          // "number"
typeof 42n         // "bigint"
typeof true        // "boolean"
typeof undefined   // "undefined"
typeof null        // "object" ← historical bug
typeof Symbol("x") // "symbol"
typeof {}          // "object"
typeof []          // "object"
typeof (() => {})  // "function"
TIP: Use Number.isNaN(x), not global isNaN(x). Global coerces first: isNaN('hello') → true. Number.isNaN('hello') → false.
Why does typeof null return 'object'?
Historical bug: early JS used bit-tags and null (all-zeros pointer) shared the object tag. Unfixable without breaking the web.
null vs undefined?
undefined: not yet assigned. null: explicit 'no value'. Never assign undefined manually; use null for intentional emptiness.
What is BigInt?
Arbitrary-precision integer. 42n or BigInt(42). Use for integers > Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53-1). Can't mix with regular numbers without conversion.
💬 Say it like this

There are eight types: seven primitives — string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol — and object, which covers arrays, functions, dates, Map and Set.

The classic trap is typeof null, which returns "object". That is an old bug from the first version of JavaScript, and it cannot be fixed without breaking existing sites.

topics.title: == vs === — explain the difference.
topics.html:
• === (strict): no coercion. Different types → always false.
  • == (loose): coerces to common type. Rule: always use ===.
  • Only good == exception: x == null (shorthand for 'null or undefined').
"5" === 5      // false (different types)
"5" == 5       // true (string coerced to number)
null == undefined // true (special-cased)
NaN === NaN    // false ← NaN is never equal to anything
[] == false    // true ([] → "" → 0; false → 0)
[] == ![]      // true (![] is false)
When is || wrong and ?? correct?
|| returns right for any falsy: 0, '', false, null, undefined, NaN. ?? returns right only for null or undefined. If 0 or empty string are valid values, you need ??.
All 7 falsy values?
false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else truthy — including '0', 'false', [], {}, any function.
💬 Say it like this

=== compares value and type, with no conversion. == converts the values first, which gives you strange results like an empty array being equal to false.

So I always use ===. The only exception I make is x == null, because it is a short way to check for null and undefined at the same time.

topics.title: What is a closure?
topics.html:
A function that remembers variables from its lexical scope even after that scope has finished executing. Every JS function is a closure.

function createCounter(initial = 0) {
  let count = initial;
  return { increment: () => ++count, getCount: () => count };
}
// Classic trap: var in loop
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); // 3 3 3
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j)); // 0 1 2
// var: function-scoped, all callbacks share the SAME i.
// let: block-scoped, each iteration creates a fresh binding.
💬 Say it like this

A closure is when a function "remembers" the variables from where it was defined, even after that outer function returned. The classic trap: var in a loop. With var, all the setTimeout callbacks share the same i variable, so they all print 3. With let, each iteration gets its own copy.

How are closures related to memory leaks?
A closure holds references to outer variables — they can't be GC'd while closure lives. Classic leak: event listener captures large object, listener never removed.

topics.title: Explain the Event Loop. Microtask vs Macrotask queue.
topics.html:
• Macrotask queue: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events. One macrotask per tick.
  • Microtask queue: Promise.then/catch/finally, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver. ALL drained before next macrotask.
  • Order per tick: sync → drain ALL microtasks → one macrotask → drain ALL microtasks → render → repeat.
console.log("start");
setTimeout(() => console.log("setTimeout"), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("promise 1")).then(() => console.log("promise 2"));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log("microtask"));
console.log("end");
// Output: start → end → promise 1 → microtask → promise 2 → setTimeout
💬 Say it like this

JS is single-threaded. When the call stack is empty, the event loop checks queues for work. Microtasks (Promises, queueMicrotask) are fully drained every time the stack empties. Macrotasks (setTimeout, events) run one at a time, with microtask draining between each.

Classic interview output: log(1); setTimeout(()=>log(2),0); Promise.resolve().then(()=>log(3)); log(4) → Answer: 1, 4, 3, 2.

What is requestAnimationFrame?
Special macrotask before next browser paint (~60 FPS). Use for animations instead of setTimeout — synced with screen refresh.
What is starvation?
Long chain of microtasks re-queuing itself → macrotasks never run → browser can't paint → frozen UI.

topics.title: What is this? Resolution rules.
topics.html:
• Determined at call time, not definition time. Exception: arrow functions.
  • Priority: new Foo() → instance. fn.call(ctx) → ctx. obj.method() → obj. plain fn() → undefined (strict) or globalThis.
  • Arrow functions don't have own this — lexically inherit from surrounding scope.
const user = {
  name: "Alex",
  greet() { return `Hi, ${this.name}`; },
  greetArrow: () => `Hi, ${this.name}`, // this is NOT user!
};
user.greet();              // "Hi, Alex"
const fn = user.greet; fn(); // "Hi, undefined" — context lost
fn.call({ name: "Max" });  // "Hi, Max"
call vs apply vs bind?
call(ctx, a, b): invoke immediately, args as list. apply(ctx, [a, b]): invoke immediately, args as array. bind(ctx): returns new function with context locked, doesn't invoke.
💬 Say it like this

In JavaScript this depends on how a function is called, not on where it is written. If I call user.greet(), this is the user. If I take that same function out and call it alone, the context is lost.

Arrow functions are the exception: they have no own this, they take it from the surrounding scope. That is why an arrow function works well inside a class method or a callback, but not as an object method.

topics.title: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any.
topics.html:
• Promise.all — waits for all. First rejection → whole thing rejects. Fail-fast.
  • Promise.allSettled — waits for all, returns status of each. Never rejects.
  • Promise.race — resolves/rejects with first settled promise.
  • Promise.any — resolves with first fulfilled. Rejects only if all fail (AggregateError).
// Parallel, fail-fast:
const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([api.getUser(id), api.getPosts(id)]);
// Parallel, independent (dashboard widgets):
const results = await Promise.allSettled([api.getA(), api.getB()]);
results.forEach(r => r.status === "fulfilled" ? use(r.value) : handleError(r.reason));
💬 Say it like this

Use Promise.all when all requests must succeed — like loading user data and permissions together. If one fails, you don't want partial data. Use Promise.allSettled for a dashboard with independent widgets — if one fails, the others still render and you handle failures individually.

topics.title: Hoisting & Temporal Dead Zone
topics.html:
• var: declaration hoisted, initialization stays. Before assignment → undefined.
  • let/const: hoisted but in Temporal Dead Zone until declaration line. Accessing → ReferenceError.
  • Function declarations: hoisted completely — callable before their line.
console.log(x); // undefined (var declaration hoisted)
var x = 5;
// console.log(y); // ReferenceError — TDZ
let y = 10;
greet(); // "Hello!" — function declaration fully hoisted
function greet() { console.log("Hello!"); }
// sayBye(); // TypeError — sayBye is undefined here
var sayBye = () => console.log("Bye!");
💬 Say it like this

Hoisting means declarations are known before the code runs. With var the variable exists from the start but its value is undefined. With let and const the variable also exists, but you cannot touch it before the declaration line — that is the temporal dead zone, and you get a ReferenceError.

Function declarations are hoisted completely, so you can call them before they appear in the file. In practice I just use const and declare things before I use them, and the whole topic disappears.

topics.title: Garbage collection & most common memory leaks.
topics.html:
• Core concept: reachability. Values stay in memory while reachable from roots (globalThis, call stack, active closures).
  • Algorithm: Mark-and-Sweep. Start from roots, walk all references, mark reachable. Sweep (free) everything unmarked.

Most common leaks:

  1. Forgotten event listeners — listener's closure holds data alive.
  2. Forgotten timers — setInterval never cleared.
  3. Detached DOM nodes — removed from DOM but referenced in JS variable.
  4. Global variables — accidentally on window, never collected.
  5. Closures capturing too much — handler closes over giant object, only needs one field.
  6. Module-level caches growing unbounded — Map keyed by userId never cleaned.
// LEAK: scroll listener captures bigData, never removed
window.addEventListener("scroll", () => console.log(bigData.length));

// FIX in React: useEffect cleanup handles this
useEffect(() => {
  const onScroll = () => { /* ... */ };
  window.addEventListener("scroll", onScroll);
  return () => window.removeEventListener("scroll", onScroll);
}, []);
💬 Say it like this

GC works by reachability — if an object can't be reached from running code, it gets collected. The engine marks everything reachable from known roots, then frees the rest.

The most common leak I've hit is forgetting to remove event listeners. The listener holds a reference to its closure, and the closure holds everything it captured. In React, useEffect cleanup handles this automatically — if you write it correctly.

How do you detect memory leaks?
Chrome DevTools → Memory → Heap snapshot. Snapshot → perform action 10x → snapshot → diff. Linear growth = leak. Look for detached DOM nodes.

topics.title: WeakMap vs Map.
topics.html:
• Map: strong references to keys — keeps keys alive forever.
  • WeakMap: weak references — if key object has no other references, GC collects it and entry vanishes automatically.
  • Constraints: keys must be objects. Not iterable. No .size.
// LEAK: Map keeps removed DOM elements alive
const cache = new Map();
// FIX: WeakMap — entry vanishes when el is removed from DOM
const cache = new WeakMap<Element, Metadata>();

// WeakSet: track 'seen' objects without preventing GC
function deepWalk(obj: object, visited = new WeakSet()) {
  if (visited.has(obj)) return; // cycle detected
  visited.add(obj);
}
TIP: 'WeakRef exists but MDN says to avoid it unless you have a strong reason. For 99% of app code, WeakMap is the right tool.'
💬 Say it like this

A Map keeps a strong reference to its keys, so if I use DOM nodes as keys, those nodes can never be garbage collected — that is a memory leak.

A WeakMap holds the keys weakly. When nothing else points to the object, the garbage collector removes it and the entry disappears by itself. The price is that keys must be objects, and you cannot iterate a WeakMap or read its size.

topics.title: Explain prototypal inheritance.
topics.html:
• JS inherits object from object. Every object has [[Prototype]] link.
  • Property lookup: object itself → prototype → Object.prototype → null.
  • class is syntactic sugar over prototype chains.
class Animal {
  #secret = "hidden"; // true private field (ES2022)
  constructor(name: string) { this.name = name; }
  speak() { return `${this.name} speaks`; }
}
const dog = new Animal("Rex");
Object.getPrototypeOf(dog) === Animal.prototype; // true
f.__proto__ === Foo.prototype; // true
f.__proto__.__proto__ === Object.prototype; // true
f.__proto__.__proto__.__proto__ === null; // end of chain
💬 Say it like this

In JavaScript objects inherit from other objects. Every object has a hidden link to its prototype, and when you read a property the engine looks at the object first, then at its prototype, and so on until it reaches null.

The class keyword is just nicer syntax over the same prototype chain. It does not add a new inheritance model.

topics.title: Explain map, filter, reduce.
topics.html:
• map: transform each element → same-length array.
  • filter: keep elements matching predicate → shorter or equal length.
  • reduce: fold array into single value. Most powerful, most misused.
const users = [{ id:1,name:"Alice",age:28,active:true },{ id:2,name:"Bob",age:17,active:false }];
const names = users.map(u => u.name);               // ["Alice", "Bob"]
const adults = users.filter(u => u.age >= 18);      // Alice
const totalAge = users.reduce((acc,u) => acc+u.age, 0); // 45

// Immutable-style updates (important for React state)
const add = [...arr, newItem];
const remove = arr.filter(i => i.id !== id);
const update = arr.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, ...patch } : i);
// flatMap = map + flat(1) in one pass
const sentences = ["hello world", "foo bar"];
sentences.flatMap(s => s.split(" ")); // ["hello","world","foo","bar"]
sort() gotchas?
Default sort is lexicographic: [10,2,1].sort() → [1,10,2]. Always pass comparator for numbers: nums.sort((a,b) => a-b). sort() mutates in place — spread first if you need immutability.
💬 Say it like this

map transforms every element and returns an array of the same length. filter keeps the elements that match a condition. reduce folds the whole array into one value.

In React I use them mostly for immutable updates: spread to add, filter to remove, map to update one item. That way I always create a new array, which is exactly what React needs to see a change.

topics.title: ESM vs CommonJS — key differences.
topics.html:
// CommonJS
const fs = require("fs"); // sync, runtime resolution
module.exports = { foo, bar };
// ES Modules (ESM)
import fs from "fs"; // static, analysed at parse time
export const foo = () => {};
// Key: ESM = static analysis → tree-shaking works. CJS = dynamic → no tree-shaking.
// Dynamic import — lazy load on demand
const { parseCSV } = await import("./csv-parser.js");
// In React:
const HeavyChart = React.lazy(() => import("./HeavyChart"));
💬 Say it like this

CommonJS uses require and resolves modules at runtime. ES modules use import and are analysed statically, before the code runs.

That difference is why tree-shaking only works properly with ES modules — the bundler can see which exports are actually used. And dynamic import() is what I use for code splitting, for example with React.lazy for a heavy chart.

topics.title: Iterators, Generators & for...of
topics.html:
// Generator — simple range
function* range(start: number, end: number) {
  for (let i = start; i <= end; i++) yield i;
}
for (const n of range(1, 5)) console.log(n); // 1 2 3 4 5
// Async generator — for streaming data
async function* streamLines(url: string) {
  const reader = (await fetch(url)).body!.getReader();
  // ...yield lines as they arrive
}
for await (const line of streamLines("/api/stream")) { console.log(line); }
💬 Say it like this

A generator is a function that can pause and continue. Each yield returns a value and stops until you ask for the next one, so you can produce values lazily instead of building a big array.

I do not write them often in application code. Where they are really useful is streaming: an async generator plus for await lets me process data as it arrives, for example lines from a server response.

topics.title: Error Handling — Custom errors & Result pattern.
topics.html:
class ApiError extends Error {
  constructor(message: string, public readonly statusCode: number, public readonly endpoint: string) {
    super(message); this.name = "ApiError";
    Object.setPrototypeOf(this, ApiError.prototype);
  }
}
try { await api.login(credentials); }
catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof ApiError) { if (err.statusCode === 401) redirect("/login"); }
  else throw err; // re-throw unexpected
}
// Result pattern — avoid exceptions for expected failures
type Result<T, E = Error> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };
💬 Say it like this

I separate expected failures from unexpected ones. A failed login or a validation error is normal, so I return it as data — that is the Result pattern, and TypeScript then forces me to handle both cases.

For real exceptions I use custom error classes like ApiError with a status code, so the catch block can check instanceof and decide what to do. If the error is not mine, I re-throw it instead of swallowing it.
